title: Caro-Kann Bonus Lines
description: In this bonus course, you receive several more suggested variations for your repertoire, so that you can choose specific lines to play in your Caro-Kann!

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n5/2bpP3/8/2N2N2/PP2BP.text:
And we castle ourselves. 

We may even have ideas of ...d4.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1p2n/2bpP3/5P2/3BBN2/P.text:
White manages to place their bishop on e3, aiming to trade bishops.

We accept the trade.

r1bq1rk1/pp4pp/2n1pp1n/3pP3/5P2/3BQN2/PP.text: We'll go for our plan of undermining the center with ...f6.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2bpP3/5P2/3B1N2/PP.text:
White’s position isn’t bad, but it’s hard to castle kingside because of the premature f4. 

We make a flexible developing move, 7...Nh6, to keep our king safe after castling, and we’ll soon start breaking up White’s center with ...f6.

Remember that ...Nh6 is a great move in most f4 setups.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n5/2bpP3/8/2N2N2/PP2BPP.text: White develops their light-squared bishop to e2, getting ready to castle.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1p2n/2bpP3/5P2/3B1N2/PP.text:
White may try to trade bishops by protecting the e3 square with the queen, since our bishop on c5 is very strong. 

We simply castle.

r1bqkb1r/pp2nppp/4p3/2npP3/8/3B1N2/PPP2P.text:
Maneuvering the other knight to c6 via e7 is a nice way to develop it around the annoying e5 pawn.

We will take on d3, play ...Nc6 and ...Be7/Bd7 with a very solid position. 

Castling short and then playing on the queenside (...Rc8, ...Qb6) are plausible ideas.

r1bqkbnr/3n1ppp/4p3/2PpP3/8/4B3/P4PPP/RN.text: After 9...Nd7 the c5-pawn will fall shortly and once we complete our development in full we will be in great shape.

r1bqkbnr/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2PpP3/8/3B1N2/PPP2.text:
White reinforces the e5 pawn with the knight, but this gives us a clear target - the bishop on d3. 

We challenge it immediately after capturing on c5 with the knight.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2npP3/8/3B1N2/PPP2PP.text: White castles their king into safety.

rn2kb2/pp1b2p1/4pq1r/2Pp4/6Qp/2N2N2/PPP2.text:
We calmly finish development with 11...Bd7, reaching a very promising position. 

We’ll capture on c5 with our bishop, play ...Nc6, and castle long, with the added possibility of ...e5, creating a discovered attack on the queen.

rnb1kb2/pp4p1/4pq1r/2Pp4/6Qp/2N2N2/PPP2P.text: White develops their knight, blocking the attack on b2.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/4p3/2bPP3/8/8/PP3PPP/RNB.text:
Capturing on d5 seems to be White’s main idea.

We recapture with our e-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/4p3/2bpP3/5P2/5N2/PPP3PP.text:
White develops logically. 

We do the same, also bringing our knight out.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/8/2bpP3/8/5N2/PP3PPP/RNB.text:
White keeps developing naturally. 

We do the same, with 7...Ne7. Our pieces come out easily.

rnbqk2r/pp2nppp/8/2bpP3/8/2N2N2/PP3PPP/R.text:
Play continues with normal developing moves on both sides. 

We continue by developing our b-knight to c6.

rnbqkb1r/pp3pp1/4p2B/2PpP3/6Qp/8/PPP2PPP.text:
If White insists on staying along the g-file then taking our knight is the only way.

We recapture with the rook.

rnbqkb2/pp3pp1/4p2r/2PpP3/6Qp/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
White develops a piece, 9.Nf3, also pressuring our h4 pawn. 

But we gain another tempo by attacking the queen again. 9...f5 is our next move.

rnbqkb2/pp4p1/4pP1r/2Pp4/6Qp/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
White captures our f5 pawn en passant, removing the threat to the queen. 

We recapture on f6 with the queen, which now occupies an excellent square since the annoying e5 pawn is gone.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/4p3/2PpP3/1P6/8/P4PPP/RN.text:
The recapture on b4 is forced. 

Our key idea now makes White’s entire plan fall apart, 7...b6 is next.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/4p3/p1PpP3/1P6/2P5/P4PPP.text:
White tries to keep the chain together, but it collapses quickly.

We capture on b4 without hesitation.

rnbqkbnr/5ppp/1p2p3/2PpP3/1P6/4B3/P4PPP/.text:
White keeps trying to defend, now with a bishop move, but it’s futile.

We capture on c5, dismantling the pawn chain completely.

rnbqkbnr/5ppp/4p3/2PpP3/8/4B3/P4PPP/RN1Q.text:
White captures back with the c-pawn.

Instead, if 9. Bxc5 we recapture 9...Bxc5 10. bxc5.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White takes the center with 2.d4.

We immediately challenge it with 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
The Advance Variation appears after 3.e5. 

We counterattack against d4 with 3...c5, striking back in the center.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2PpP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.text:
White grabs the critical pawn on c5. 

In the 4...Nc6 line, we sometimes don’t get the pawn back for a while, which isn’t to everyone’s taste. 

After 4...e6, we’ll recover it soon enough.

rnbqkbnr/pp3pp1/4p3/2PpP2p/8/6Q1/PPP2PPP.text:
White insists on attacking our g7-pawn. 

So we keep chasing the queen, 6...h4.

rnbqkbnr/pp3pp1/4p3/2PpP3/6Qp/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White continues to insist, keeping pressure on g7. 

We respond by attacking the queen again, developing with tempo through 7...Nh6.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2PpP3/1P6/8/P1P2PPP/.text:
Trying to hold onto the pawn with 5.b4 is ill-advised because White’s pawn chain is too vulnerable. 

Still, this mistake is common in online play - expect to see it around 17% of the time. 

We immediately begin softening up the pawn chain with 5...a5.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2PpP3/2P5/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
White attacks our center with 5.c4 but we can simply ignore this thrust and continue our development. 

It’s played in only about 4% of games.

We immediately capture the c5 pawn with the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2PpP3/5P2/8/PPP3PP/R.text:
White is defending the wrong pawn! 

At this point, 5.f4 is rare, it appears only about 3% of games. 

We respond by taking on c5.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2PpP3/6Q1/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White tries to stop us from recapturing on c5 with 5.Qg4, but we’ll use that exposed queen as a target. 

It’s a rare try, only about 1% of games, yet tricky enough to appear in practice.

We respond with 5...h5, trying to chase the queen from attacking g7.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2PpP3/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/.text:
5.Bd3 is a natural developing move, but one we can exploit precisely.

It’s quite rare, appearing in only about 1% of games. 

We’re in no rush to recapture on c5 just yet, and we prepare it with 5...Nd7.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
I want to give you a second weapon for the Advance Caro–Kann: 4...e6.

This move leads to a more solid type of gameplay than 4...Nc6. The choice is yours, depending on your style. 

In this section of bonus lines, you’ll find plenty of viable secondary weapons you can use against White, depending on your needs. 

Time for 1.e4, to which we respond with the Caro–Kann.

r1b2r2/pp4kp/1bn2pn1/4p3/1PB5/P1N2N2/1B3.text: As mentioned, it's time for us to push our e-pawn, getting a strong central pawn formation and preparing to go for ...Bg4.

r1b2rk1/pp5p/1bn1ppn1/8/1PB5/P4N2/1B3PPP.text:
White recaptures with the rook. 

Our next idea is to get the king out of the pin with 15...Kg7, freeing ourselves to push the e-pawn next.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/1bn1p1n1/3pP3/1P6/P2B1N2.text:
White reinforces the powerful e5 pawn with the rook. 

We strike back with the ...f6 pawn break, aiming to free our pieces and challenge the center.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1p1n1/2bpP3/8/3B1NB1/P.text:
With 10.Nbd2, we reach a typical structure for this line. 

We have an interesting idea for counterplay here, 10...f5, gaining space and threatening to trap the bishop on g3.

r1bq1rk1/pp4pp/1bn1pPn1/3p4/1P6/P2B1N2/1.text:
White has to concede the space and captures on f6.

We recapture with the g-pawn and gain a powerful central formation that forces White to react quickly.

r1bq1rk1/pp4pp/2n1pPn1/2bp4/8/3B1NB1/PPP.text: White takes en passant, stopping the advance of the f-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/pp5p/1bn1ppn1/3p4/1PP5/P2B1N2/1.text:
13.c4 is definitely White’s best try to challenge our center. 

I like this straightforward approach, taking on c4, though the alternative 13...Nf4 14.Bf1 e5 is also interesting.

r1bq1rk1/pp5p/1bn1ppn1/8/1PB5/P4N2/1B3PP.text:
White takes on c4 with the bishop.

Our king is slightly exposed, so we trade queens. 14...Qxd1 is our move.

r1bq1rk1/pp5p/2n1ppn1/2bp4/8/3B1NB1/PPPN.text:
Recapturing with the g-pawn is an interesting recapture. 

We weaken our king a bit but in turn get a powerful mobile pawn formation.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/1bn1p3/3pP3/1P6/P4N2/1BP.text:
Moves like Bd3 and Bb2 are interchangeable, but they often appear in some order. 

We continue our development, 8...Nge7 is next.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2bpP3/1P3P2/P7/2P3.text:
White stays consistent with their plan and attacks our bishop with 7.b4. 

As usual, we simply retreat to b6, keeping the bishop safe and well placed.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2bpP3/1P6/P4N2/2P2.text:
White’s plan after 5.a3 was to push b4 once we recaptured on c5, and now it’s on the board with 7.b4. 

We calmly retreat our bishop to b6, escaping danger.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2bpP3/8/3B1N2/PPP2.text:
Castling is a logical move. 

White can play a3 at any point which will take us to the main line.

We also continue developing our pieces, 7...Nge7, getting ready to castle.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/1bn1p3/3pP3/1P6/P2B1N2/1.text:
Now we see White’s strategy unfold after 9.Bd3. 

We must block the dangerous bishop to prevent a potential Greek Gift sacrifice on h7, so we place our e7 knight on g6.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/2bpP3/5B2/3B1N2/PP.text:
White goes for 8.Bf4, this being the most popular a3-less line. 

Our key move is 8...Ng6, which not only attacks f4 and e5 but also prevents any Greek Gift ideas (Bxh7+) after we castle.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/1bn1p1n1/3pP3/1P6/P2B1N2/.text:
White castles their king. 

We also castle, bringing our king to safety.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/1bn1p2n/3pP3/1P3P2/P4N2/2.text:
Our last move of the variation is a nice developing one, 8...Nh6. 

White will not find it easy to castle and we can launch a quick strike with ...f6 in the near future.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1p1n1/2bpP3/8/3B1NB1/PP.text:
White escapes the threat by retreating the bishop to g3. 

We castle, bringing our king to safety.

r1bqkbnr/1p1n1ppp/2P1p3/pP1p4/8/P7/1BP2P.text:
White pushes their c-pawn, the only way to keep it for now.

We respond by taking on c6.

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/2n1p3/pPPpP3/8/P7/2P2PPP.text:
Pushing the b-pawn again, attacking our knight, might look tempting.

But we just get our pawn back by taking on e5 with the knight.

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/4p3/pPPpn3/8/P7/1BP2PPP/.text:
White continues developing and places the bishop on the long diagonal - consistent, but the queenside pawns are overextended. 

We retreat the knight to d7, targeting the c5 pawn.

r1bqkbnr/3n1ppp/2P1p3/p2p4/8/P7/1BP2PPP/.text: White recaptures on c6, attacking our knight.

r1bqkbnr/5ppp/2P1pn2/p2p4/8/P7/1BP2PPP/R.text:
Our knight's journey looks a little peculiar but we are ready to proceed with moves such as ...Qb6/Bc5/Ne7 and ...Ba6 if need be. 

The c6-pawn is going to fall.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpP3/1P6/P7/2P2PP.text:
This move looks consistent with a3 but it's mistimed because we can hammer at White's pawn chain.

However, it's the most popular, played 52% of the time here!

After 6...a5 White is going to have a hard time keeping the formation together.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpP3/5P2/P7/1PP3P.text:
White plays 6.f4, protecting the important e5 pawn. 

This move isn’t very logical and appears in only about 4% of games.

6.f4 actually helps our bishop after we capture on c5, so we do just that with 6...Bxc5, placing our bishop on an open diagonal.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpP3/8/P4N2/1PP2P.text:
The best way for White to protect e5 is 6.Nf3, played about 38% of the time. 

We immediately regain our pawn: 6...Bxc5 is next.

r2qk2r/pp1nnppp/4p3/2bpP3/8/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
We continue developing with 8...Ne7, reaching a very harmonious position. 

We’ll castle short, improve our pieces with ...Ng6 to pressure e5, and place our rook on the semi-open c-file for active play.

rn1qk1nr/pp1B1ppp/4p3/2bpP3/8/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
White exchanges, trading a more active bishop for our less useful one. 

We recapture with development, 7...Nxd7.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/4p3/1BbpP3/8/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
This dubious check has been surprisingly popular in online games, appearing in about 19% of them. 

We simply block while offering a trade of our least active piece.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/4p3/2bpP3/8/3B1N2/PPP2PP.text:
White continues developing, still delaying a3 for now. 

You're going to see this move 16% of the time.

We do the same, and our response is 6...Nc6.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/4p3/2bpP3/8/P4N2/1PP2PPP.text: This move just transposes directly into the main line.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The game begins as usual. 

We build our typical light-square pawn chain.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White plays the Advance Variation with 3.e5. 

We counter immediately against d4 in true Gotham style with 3...c5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2PpP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.text:
White takes on c5, the critical approach. 

As seen in the previous study, our idea is 4...e6, we'll get the pawn back soon enough.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2PpP3/8/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
This is also a sound developing move. White can delay a3 for a moment. 

It’s the second most popular line, played in 19% of games. 

We simply regain our pawn with 5...Bxc5.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2PpP3/8/P7/1PP2PPP/R.text:
A very nice idea from White, 5.a3, to prepare for our ...Bxc5 capture.

White's goal is to gain a tempo with b4 and then play Bb2/Bd3 with good control over the center/kingside. 

This move is the fourth most popular, and expect to see it 14% of the time.

It's the most popular among master games, though!

Our solution is to develop our b-knight, attacking e5 and giving White a chance to go wrong.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
No matter which line you choose against the 4.dxc5 Caro–Kann, this chapter is an important one. 

White’s setups with a3 have become topical and challenging over the past decade. 

The game starts with 1.e4, that means Caro time!

2rqkb1r/1p1b1ppp/p3p3/2PpPn2/1P1B4/2P2N2.text:
White’s only way to defend c5 is 11.b4. 

We now unleash a very nice pawn sacrifice with 11...b6. 

We’ll be down a pawn, but our active pieces and White’s weakened queenside give us ample compensation.

2rqkb1r/3b1ppp/pP2p3/3pP3/1P1Q4/2P2N2/P4.text: White recaptures with the queen, still trying to hold everything together.

2rqkb1r/3b1ppp/pP2p3/3pPn2/1P1B4/2P2N2/P.text:
White captures on b6 - otherwise we win c5 back easily. 

First we eliminate the key defender with 12...Nxd4, clearing the way to recapture on b6.

3qkb1r/3b1ppp/pP2p3/3pP3/1PrQ4/2P2N2/P4P.text:
We finish with 13...Rc4, a precise move kicking away the queen. 

Our active pieces, queenside targets, and bishop pair give us full compensation once we take on b6. 

We can even toss in ...Re4+ to make White lose castling rights.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/1q2p3/2npP3/3Q4/5N2/PPPN.text:
White develops with 9.Nbd2, keeping the option of castling long. 

We also develop with 9...Ne7, not only preparing to castle but also getting ready to attack the queen.

r1b1k2r/pp2nppp/1q2p3/2npP3/3Q4/1N3N2/PP.text:
White plays 10.Nb3, pressuring our knight on c5 and aiming to open the a-file for the rook. 

We’re forced to take on b3.

r1b1k2r/pp2nppp/1q2p3/3pP3/3Q4/1P3N2/1PP.text:
White recaptures with the a-pawn. 

We trade queens with 11...Qxd4, an equal and natural exchange.

r1b1k2r/pp2nppp/4p3/3pP3/3N4/1P6/1PP2PPP.text:
White recaptures with the knight. 

We play 12...Ng6, putting pressure on e5 and forcing White onto the defensive.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/4p1n1/3pP3/8/1P3N2/1PP2PP.text: White retreats the knight to f3, a necessary move to support the e5 pawn.

r1b1k2r/pp4pp/4ppn1/3pP3/8/1P3N2/1PP2PPP.text:
Now comes 13...f6! 

White is forced to trade, and after the exchanges we’ll achieve an excellent position with a strong, healthy center.

r1b1kb1r/1p1B1ppp/p3p3/q1PpPn2/3B4/2N2N2.text:
White captures on d7, giving up the bishop for the knight. 

If White retreats instead, we simply take on c5. 

We recapture and develop at the same time, 10...Bxd7.

r1b1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/qBPpPn2/3B4/2N2N2/.text:
White is forced to block with the knight to avoid losing the b5-bishop. 

We now get rid of the pin. 9...a6 comes next.

r1bq1rk1/1p1nbppp/4p3/pBPpP3/1P6/2P1PN2/.text:
We do the same. 

Our kingside development is complete, and we’re ready to play ...Qc7 to pressure both e5 and c5. 

We can also prepare ...b6 later to open more files and diagonals for our pieces.

White may be up a pawn, but with all their pawns weak, we have excellent compensation.

r1bqk1nr/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2BpP3/8/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
White trades bishops by taking on c5. 

We recapture with the knight.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/4p3/2npP3/3Q4/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
8.Qd4 is the most played move among experienced players. 

Most other moves can be met with the simple ...Ne7 and ...0-0, along with ...Bd7/Rc8. 

Here we defend our knight actively with the queen. 8...Qb6 is our move.

r1bqk2r/1p1nbppp/4p3/pBPpP3/1P6/2P1PN2/P.text: White castles short, bringing the king to safety.

r1bqkb1r/1p1Bnppp/p3p3/2PpP3/8/2P1B3/PP3.text:
White captures on d7, trading the bishop for the knight. 

If White had played 8.Ba4 instead, then after ...Nc6 we’d be able to capture on e5 or c5. 

We recapture with our light-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/1p1n1ppp/4p3/pBPpP3/1P6/2P1PN2/.text:
White reinforces with 10.c3, necessary to defend b4. 

We simply continue developing with 10...Be7.

r1bqkb1r/1p2nppp/4p3/p1Pp4/1P6/2P1BQ2/P4.text:
We finish the variation with 9...Ne7.

The knight will soon jump to an attractive square like c6 or f5 before we complete kingside development.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/1BPpP3/1P6/4PN2/P1.text:
White recaptures, forced to accept the doubled pawns. 

Next we strike with 9...a5!, attacking the pawn chain immediately.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/1BPpPn2/1P6/4BN2/P.text:
Playing 8.b4 looks ugly, but it’s the only way for White to hang on to the extra pawn at this point. 

We’re happy to grab the bishop and double White’s pawns, 8...Nxe3 is our next move.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/1BPpPn2/3B4/5N2/PP.text:
Planting the bishop on d4 to keep everything protected is not the best, but it is the most common response. 

It’s time for us to give a check with the queen, 8...Qa5+, preventing any b4 ideas and adding more pressure to c5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1nnppp/4p3/1BPpP3/8/2P1B3/PP3.text:
With 7.c3, White hopes to either push b4 or place the bishop on d4, creating a kind of mega pawn–bishop chain. 

You’ll see this move in about 19% of games. 

We continue with 7...a6, asking White to resolve the pin.

r1bqkb1r/pp1nnppp/4p3/1BPpP3/8/4BN2/PPP2.text:
White develops naturally, 7.Nf3, but this doesn’t stop our ...Nf5 idea - it’s played 38% of the time. 

So we execute our plan with 7...Nf5, targeting the bishop on e3.

r1bqkbnr/pp1n1ppp/4p3/1BPpP3/8/4B3/PPP2P.text:
The battle continues as White refuses to give up the pawn, pinning our knight to the king with 6.Bb5. 

This is by far the most common reply, played in half of all games. 

We develop the other knight to e7, preparing our key idea of ...Nf5 to destabilize the bishop on e3.

r1bqkbnr/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2PpP3/1P6/4B3/P1P2.text:
6.b4 is a mistake, as White is giving up an important central pawn. 

And this mistake is played 17% of the time! 

We immediately regain the pawn with the knight, restoring material equality.

r1bqkbnr/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2PpP3/8/4BN2/PPP2P.text:
White gives up on the dream of keeping the extra pawn and simply develops with 6.Nf3. 

This isn’t a bad move, but it’s nothing to be afraid of - you’ll see it about 18% of the time. 

We immediately capture on c5 with the bishop, restoring material equality.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2Pp4/1P6/4BQ2/P1P2PP.text:
White recaptures with the queen. 

We follow up with 8...a5, a common and thematic undermining push.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2Ppn3/1P6/4BN2/P1P2P.text:
White may offer a trade of knights.

We accept it with 7...Nxf3+.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/p3p3/2PpPn2/3B4/2P2N2/P.text:
White plants the bishop on d4, sticking to the setup - and it looks like we’ll remain a pawn down. 

But we activate with ...Rc8, still aiming to attack the c5 pawn.

r2qkb1r/1p1bnppp/p3p3/2PpP3/8/2P1BN2/PP3.text:
White develops naturally with 9.Nf3, getting just one move away from castling. 

Our whole plan comes to life with 9...Nf5, targeting the dark-squared bishop and opening up our own bishop’s scope.

r3kb1r/1p1b1ppp/p3p3/2qpP3/3N4/2N5/PPP2P.text:
After 12...Qxc5 we’ve recovered the pawn and kept the bishop pair. 

We’ll castle next and begin queenside play, and a timely ...f6 can be strong to open diagonals for our bishops.

r3kb1r/1p1b1ppp/p3p3/q1PpP3/3N4/2N5/PPP2.text: White recaptures with the knight, the logical move.

r3kb1r/1p1b1ppp/p3p3/q1PpPn2/3B4/2N2N2/P.text:
White castles short - there’s nothing better. 

Before taking on c5, we grab the bishop pair, so we take on d4.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White takes the center with 2.d4. 

With 2...d5 we build our typical light-square pawn chain.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White goes for the Advance Caro with 3.e5. 

Our solution doesn’t change - we counter the center with our Gotham-style antidote, 3...c5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2PpP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.text:
White takes on c5, entering the greedy main line. 

As we’ve seen throughout this bonus-lines Advance Caro chapter, our remedy is 4...e6, opening up the dark-squared bishop to target c5.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2PpP3/8/4B3/PPP2PPP/.text:
White develops the dark-squared bishop to e3, trying to keep the pawn. This move appears 28% of the time and is the most popular. 

We respond with 5...Nd7, insisting on recovering the pawn quickly.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Our final study of the chapter deals with the historically most common (and greediest!) idea: 5.Be3, where White tries to hold onto the extra pawn. 

White starts the game with 1.e4, best by test.

As always our response is… the Caro.

r1bq1r1k/pp2p1bp/2n2ppn/3p4/3P1B2/2PB1N1.text:
White creates luft for the king with 11.h3.

We continue with 11...Nf7, preparing to push e5.

r1bq1r1k/pp2pnbp/2n2pp1/3p4/3P4/2PB1N1P/.text:
White retreats the bishop to h2, trying to avoid losing a tempo after ...e5. 

But we play it anyway, seizing control of the center.

r1bq1r1k/pp2ppbp/2n3pn/3p4/3P1B2/2PB1N2/.text:
White’s reply is logical, developing the b-knight to d2. 

We now execute our plan. The ...f6–Nf7 maneuver comes next.

r1bq1r1k/pp3nbp/2n2pp1/3pP3/8/2PB1N1P/PP.text:
White takes on e5, since they need to avoid getting forked.

We recapture with the f-pawn, maintaining a strong center.

r1bq1r1k/pp3nbp/2n3p1/1B1p4/4p3/2P2N1P/P.text:
But we strike back in the center with 14...e4. 

Our position becomes extremely powerful, with all our pieces ready for action.

r1bq1r1k/pp3nbp/2n3p1/1B1pp3/8/2P2N1P/PP.text: White escapes the fork threat with 14.Bb5 and tries to win the e5 pawn.

r1bq1r1k/pp3nbp/2n3p1/3pp3/8/2PB1N1P/PP1.text: We recapture with the f-pawn, maintaining a strong center

r1bq1rk1/pp2p1bp/2n2ppn/3p4/3P1B2/2PB1N2.text: White slides the rook to the semi-open e-file, trying to clamp down on e5, but it’s already too late.

r1bq1rk1/pp2pnbp/2n2pp1/3p4/3P1B2/2PB1N2.text: We end the variation by bringing our knight back to f7, reaching a great position - the ...e5 break is now completely unstoppable.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3pn/3p4/3P1B2/2PB1N2/.text:
Now comes an important moment. 

White plays 9.Nbd2, blocking the queen’s vision along the d-file. 

This allows us to strike with the powerful 9...f6! 

If White had played 9.Re1 instead, ...f6 would be riskier due to the strong 10.c4! followed by Nc3. 

In that case, 9...Bf5 would be safer, planning to recapture with the knight.

White plays 9.Re1, controlling the e5 square. 

As mentioned, the safest move is ...Bf5, since after 9...f6, White can reply with the strong 10.c4!. 

However, we have a creative idea to prepare ...f6. 

First, we safeguard the king by tucking it into the corner with 9...Kh8, and only then do we play ...f6 with the king better placed.

r1bqk1nr/pp2p1bp/2n2pp1/3p4/3P1B2/2PB3P/.text:
Suppose White develops with 8.Ne2 - 8.Nf3 looks better, but then ...e5! followed by ...e4! creates a powerful fork. 

With 8...e5, we establish a dominating center.

r1bqk1nr/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/3p4/3P1B2/2PB1N2/.text:
White follows suit with 7.Nf3 in about 48% of games. 

We respond with the unusual yet thematic 7...Nh6! 

This entire system is unconventional: this move supports the f5 square for ...Bf5 and prepares the surprising ...Nf7 retreat, supporting a later ...e5.

r1bqk1nr/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/3p4/3P1B2/2PB3P/P.text:
If White tries to stop ...Bg4 ideas with 7.h3 before playing Nf3, we have a rude surprise. 

This move appears in about 8% of games. 

After 7...f6, there’s suddenly no way to stop ...e5, and we’ll completely dominate the center.

r1bqk1nr/pp4bp/2n2pp1/3pp3/3P4/2PB3P/PP2.text: White goes back to h2 with their dark-squared bishop, a sad retreat.

r1bqk2r/pp2n1bp/2n2pp1/3pp3/3P4/2PB3P/PP.text:
We have a much better position because our pawns are dominating the board. 

Our last move is developing our g-knight to e7, getting ready to castle.

The light-squared bishop can develop to e6, and our center stands strong.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2n3pn/3p4/3P1B2/2PB1N2/P.text:
White reacts calmly, bringing their king to safety.

We castle as well.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pp1p/2n3p1/3p4/3P1B2/2PB4/PP.text:
If White starts with Bf4, that gives us extra motivation to push ...e5 with tempo. 

In the next study, we’ll look at 6.Nf3.

For now, we continue with normal development, 6...Bg7 is next.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3p4/3P4/2PB4/PP3PPP.text:
After 5.c3, we introduce our twist with an unusual move, 5...g6! 

The main idea is to prepare ...Bf5 while opening the g-file for potential attacking chances. 

Another key concept is to control the e5 square with ...Bg7 and ...f6.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White places a second pawn in the center, 2.d4. 

We continue with 2...d5, exactly what the doctor ordered.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3P4/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White captures on d5, entering the Exchange Variation. 

We recapture with the c-pawn, keeping a pawn in the center and reaching the classic Carlsbad structure.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3P4/3B4/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White goes for the main line. with 4.Bd3. 

Other deviations were dealt with in the main Caro-Kann Course.

We immediately challenge the d4 pawn by playing 4...Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
This is a bonus study where I want to share an interesting and rarer setup against the Exchange Variation. 

If you’re looking for a more aggressive and surprising reaction, this is it!

White starts the game with 1.e4 - so far so good. 

As always, we respond with the Caro-Kann.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pp1p/2n3p1/3p4/3P4/2PB1N2/PP.text:
White develops the knight and prepares to castle - a good plan. 

Without hesitation, we offer the trade, 6...Bf5 is our next move.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3p4/3P4/2PB4/PP3PPP.text:
White defends the pawn by playing 5.c3. 

Now it’s time to explore our ...Bf5 ideas. 5...g6 comes next.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/3p4/3P1B2/2PQ1N1P.text:
White chooses 11.h3, creating an escape square for the king and bishop. 

It’s not a forced move, but the game would continue similarly either way.

r2q1rk1/pp3pbp/2n1pnp1/3p4/3P1B2/2PQ1N1P.text:
We end the variation with 11...e6, building our pawns on strong light squares. 

Not only is this a typical Caro–Kann idea, but it’s also logical since we’ve traded our light-squared bishop. 

From here, we should aim to play on the queenside with ideas like ...Rc8 and ...Na5–Nc4. A timely ...Qb6 can also be annoying for White, and we can reroute the knight from f6 to e8–d6 or back to d7 to control key squares such as e5.

r2qk1nr/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/3p4/3P1B2/2PQ1N2/P.text:
White develops as well, bringing the dark-squared bishop out to f4. 

We continue with kingside development, bringing the undeveloped knight to c6 - now only one move away from castling.

r2qk1nr/pp3p1p/2nBp3/3p1p2/3P4/2P2N2/PP1.text:
White trades on d6.

We’re forced to recapture with the queen.

r2qk2r/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/3p4/3P1B2/2PQ1N2/P.text:
White plays another standard developing move, 10.Nbd2. 

As mentioned, our next move is to castle - safe and sound.

r2qkbnr/pp2pp1p/2n3p1/3p1B2/3P4/2P2N2/PP.text:
White may be tempted to double our pawns by trading on f5 - and indeed does so in more than 51% of games. 

We’re forced to recapture with the g-pawn, but in return we gain strong control over the e4 square and an open g-file for future pressure.

r2qkbnr/pp2pp1p/2n3p1/3p1b2/3P4/2PB1N2/P.text:
Chess isn’t checkers, so White isn’t obligated to capture on f5 and instead castles.

This happens about 33% of the time. 

We make the trade ourselves with 7...Bxd3.

r2qkbnr/pp2pp1p/2n3p1/3p4/3P4/2PQ1N2/PP3.text:
White is forced to recapture with the queen. 

We simply continue developing with 8...Bg7.

r2qkbnr/pp2pp1p/2n5/3p1p2/3P1B2/2P2N2/PP.text:
White continues developing normally with 8.Bf4. 

We answer with 8...e6, building a “tree” pawn setup on the light squares and preparing to develop our bishop to d6.

r2qkbnr/pp3p1p/2n1p3/3p1p2/3P1B2/2P2N2/P.text:
White reasonably continues developing with 9.Nbd2. 

We also develop with 9...Bd6, gaining a tempo by attacking the dark-squared bishop.

r3k1nr/pp3p1p/2nqp3/3p1p2/3P4/2P2N2/PP1N.text: White castles short, a natural move, but it gives us a clear target, especially with the open g-file at our disposal.

r3k2r/pp3p1p/2nqpn2/3p1p2/3P4/2P2N2/PP1N.text:
We finish the variation with 11...Nf6, and I really like our position here. 

We’ll follow up with ...Ne4 and then ...Rg8 becomes highly tempting. 

Our king can safely tuck away on the queenside, while White will face enormous pressure along the open g-file.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White takes the center. 

We love the center just as much, so we counter with 2...d5, building our typical light-squared pawn chain.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3P4/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The Exchange Variation appears after 3.exd5. 

We recapture in our standard way, 3...cxd5, keeping a solid structure.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3P4/3B4/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The main line continues.

We develop our knight to c6, immediately attacking the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In the previous study, we looked at the aggressive ...f6 and ...e5 ideas, but as I mentioned, the move ...g6 also serves to facilitate ...Bf5. Let’s see how that looks in practice.

White starts with the familiar 1.e4 formula.

We reply with the Gotham Caro, 1...c6.

lessons.title: Deviations to the Main Line Part 1: Early Sidelines

r2qk1nr/pp1n1ppp/2pbp1b1/8/2BP4/2P2NN1/P.text: White plays 9.c3, reinforcing d4, one of several natural options.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2pbpnb1/8/2BP4/2P2NN1/PP.text:
We finish the line with 9...Ngf6, reaching our typical Classical Caro setup. 

We are ready to castle and eventually push our queenside pawns for counterplay, potentially after Qc7 and Rd8.

r2qk2r/pp1nbppp/2p1pnb1/8/3P4/3B1NN1/PPP.text:
Our final move is 9...Be7, calmly developing and preparing to castle. 

In the future, we should aim for queenside play via a ...c5 break, or even a space-gaining ...a5–a4 thrust (especially if White plays b3–Bb2). 

In general, both sides have a very solid and sound position, with White enjoying slightly more space - which is why ...c5 is a key idea to regain that space, often supported by ...Qc7 or ...Qb6 and ...Rd8 or ...Rc8.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/7P/3PQ3/8/PPP2PP1.text:
The queen recaptures. 

We improve our remaining knight by placing it on f6, gaining a tempo on the queen.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/7P/3PN3/5Q2/PPP2.text:
White recaptures with the knight. 

We accept the exchange and capture on e4 again.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/7P/3PN3/5QN1/PP.text:
White continues with 9.h5, attacking the bishop. 

Now that the h-pawn is committed, we take on e4, trading our bishop for the knight.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/3P4/3B1NN1/PP.text: White activates the rook, placing it on the semi-open e-file and aligning it with our king.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2nb1/8/3P4/3B1NN1/PPP.text:
White castles short, a natural and safe developing move. 

We continue with the typical Caro idea of 8...e6, opening the diagonal for our dark-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp3pp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3P4/4Q3/PPP2PP.text:
We now play 12...h6, preventing White from playing that move themselves. 

We can continue with ...Qd5, ...Be7, and castling.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/7P/3P4/4Q3/PPP2PP1.text: The queen steps out of danger and moves to e3.

r2qkbnr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p1p1/8/3P4/6N1/PPP2P.text:
We recapture with our h-pawn. 

In exchange for our good bishop, we gain a powerful rook file, and our development will flow naturally with Ngf6, Bd6, Qc7, and potentially 0-0-0.

r2qkbnr/pp1n1ppp/2p1p1N1/8/3P4/6N1/PPP2P.text:
White trades on g6, winning the bishop pair. 

That was White’s idea all along.

r2qkbnr/pp1n1ppp/2p1p1b1/8/2BP4/5NN1/PPP.text:
White castles, a natural move in this position. 

We continue developing strongly with 8...Bd6, placing our bishop on an active diagonal.

r2qkbnr/pp1n1ppp/2p1p1b1/8/3PN2P/5QN1/PP.text:
White plays h4, trying to harass our bishop. 

We develop our kingside by bringing out our other knight to f6.

r2qkbnr/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/5b2/3PN3/5QN1/PPP.text:
White attacks our bishop with 7.N2g3. 

We can retreat to g6, although trading on e4 immediately is also acceptable. 

...Bg6 is also an idea to provoke h4–h5.

r2qkbnr/pp1npppp/2p3b1/8/2BP4/5NN1/PPP2P.text:
White can also try to place their bishop more actively with 7.Bc4, allowing our Bg6 to stay on the board. 

We blunt the bishop and prepare development with 7...e6.

r2qkbnr/pp1npppp/2p3b1/8/3P3N/6N1/PPP2PP.text:
White can also chase our bishop with 7.Nh4. 

We respond by opening the diagonal for our dark-squared bishop and queen, which now targets the knight.

r2qkbnr/pp1npppp/2p3b1/8/3P4/3B1NN1/PPP2.text:
White’s most common idea in this setup is to offer the bishop trade with 7.Bd3. 

We don’t trade and instead maintain the tension by developing our g-knight to f6, keeping the option for White to open the h-file for our rook if they decide to capture.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p1q1/5b2/3P1B2/2P2P2/.text:
We finish the line with 9...Nd7.

As Black, we’ll have the option to castle queenside or kingside. 

Just remember: if h4, play …h5, and if Ng3, play …Bc2.

rn1qk1nr/pp3ppp/2pbp1b1/8/3P1P2/5NN1/PPP.text:
We follow suit with 7...Bd6.

We plan to bring our knights out via d7 and e7, with ...Ne7 ensuring White can’t push f5 at all. 

We remain very solid with excellent light-square control and smooth development.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/3P4/2N5/PPP2P.text:
We continue with simple development, 5...Nf6. 

Interestingly, we’ve already examined this position in the Tartakower via 3...Nf6 4.Nc3 Bf5.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pN2/5b2/3P1B2/5P2/PPP.text:
White decides to trade on f6. 

We recapture with the queen; if 8.Be5, then 8...Qg6 followed by ...Nd7 is better for Black.

rn1qkbnr/pN3ppp/2p5/4pb2/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White takes the pawn on b7, the point of Nc5. 

We now play 6...Qb6, attacking the knight.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/8/3P1P2/6N1/PPP3P.text:
White chooses the aggressive 6.f4, an option played only 3% of the time, but nothing to worry about. 

We reply with the simple 6...e6, an easy way to prevent f5.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/8/3P4/5NN1/PPP2PP.text:
One of White’s most common moves is the developing move 6.Nf3. 

The main line with 6.h4 will be addressed in Studies 3 and 4, while the knight-to-f4 plans (via Nh3 or Ne2) will be studied next. 

This move occurs in roughly half of all games in this position. 

We continue developing with 6...Nd7, controlling the e5 square and limiting White’s knight jumps. 

Although 7.h4 is the most common continuation, here we focus on White’s approaches without the h4 push.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/2N2b2/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.text:
The first variation of this study appears with 5.Nc5, where White gains a tempo on the b7 pawn instead of retreating. 

This move is played only 2% of the time. 

Our solution is 5...e5, striking the center with an aggressive reaction; 5...b6 was also simple, followed by ...e6, ...Nd7, ...Bd6, and ...Ne7.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5b2/3P4/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
White can also retreat to c3, a safe move but not particularly impressive. 

This option is played only 4% of the time.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5b2/3P4/6N1/PPP2PPP.text:
Retreating the knight to g3 with tempo is White’s best and most popular option, played a massive 76% of the time. 

We simply retreat our bishop to g6, keeping it active on a strong diagonal.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5b2/3PN3/3B4/PPP2PP.text:
White chooses to protect the knight with 5.Bd3, but this comes at the cost of the d4 pawn, meaning White is either gambiting or blundering. 

This is actually the second most popular move, played 10% of the time. 

We accept the gift and capture on d4 with the queen; 5...e6 is also an option for the risk-averse.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5b2/3PN3/5P2/PPP3PP.text:
White can choose 5.f3, an anti-positional move that’s popular online but simply bad. 

White can’t develop Nf3, and the king on e1 becomes slightly loose. 

We continue with simple development, 5...e6, threatening to capture on e4 combined with …Qh4+; the plan with Nd7–Nf6 is also strong.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5b2/3PN3/5Q2/PPP2PP.text:
Among all the unusual options on move five, 5.Qf3 actually has some merit. 

White’s idea is simply to trade our Bf5 for a knight, even though the move is played only 1% of the time. 

We solve the problem with 5...e6, defending the bishop and preparing development.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5b2/4N3/3B1N2/PPP1Q.text: White steps out of the trade with 7.Qe2, lining the queen up with our king.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/5b2/3PN3/5Q2/PPP1N.text:
White plays 6.Ne2, protecting d4 and aiming for N2g3. 

Other moves like c3 or Be3 can be met with the simple ...Nd7–Ngf6. 

We continue with 6...Nd7, calmly developing; 6...Be7 was also fine. 

Even if we eventually trade our active Bf5, our structure remains solid with easy development ahead.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/5b2/3PNB2/5P2/PPP3.text:
Strong players will cover the dark squares with 6.Bf4. 

Here we simply propose a knight trade with 6...Nf6.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/5b2/4N3/3B1N2/PPP1.text:
We respond with 7...e6, preparing to trade on e4 and develop solidly with Nd7 or Nf6. 

We must develop quickly before White generates meaningful threats.

Another option was 7...Nf6!?, which looks like a blunder but isn’t thanks to the Qa5+ fork defending Bf5 - an idea we examined via transposition in the Tartakower sidelines study.

rn2k1nr/p4ppp/2p5/2q1pb2/8/8/PPP2PPP/R1B.text:
We recapture with the queen, restoring material balance.

We are ahead in development and will continue with ...Nf6 and ...0-0. If White tries 9.Bd3, then e4! is strong.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p1q1/5b2/3P1B2/2P2P2/P.text: White defends the pawn by pushing it one square.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pq2/5b2/3P1B2/5P2/PPP1.text:
The move f3 makes development awkward, forcing the knight to come out via e2, which blocks the light-squared bishop. 

We slide our queen to g6, targeting c2.

rn2kbnr/p4ppp/1qp5/2N1pb2/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White’s only retreat is back to c5. 

We capture on c5 with the bishop, looking to regain the pawn while developing.

rn2kbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5b2/3qN3/3B1N2/PPP2P.text:
White develops the knight to f3, gaining a tempo on our queen. 

We safely retreat the queen to its home square, also keeping the option to trade on e4 or d1 and enjoy our extra pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White classically controls the center with 2.d4. 

As always, we challenge it directly with 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
White develops the knight to c3, entering the Classical Variation. 

Our solution is to capture on e4, ceding some central space in exchange for smooth development.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
White recaptures the pawn. 

As mentioned in the introduction, instead of playing the Tartakower, we choose 4...Bf5, entering the Capablanca Variation. 

In this line, we aim to develop our pieces efficiently and without concessions.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the first study of our second weapon against the Classical Caro. 

Here we will analyze the historic Capablanca Variation (4...Bf5), which long served as the main line before the discoveries hidden in the Tartakower (4...Nf6). 

I’ve used this variation extensively over the years and am excited to share its ideas and nuances with you. 

The game begins with 1.e4.

We reply with 1...c6, preparing the Caro pawn chain.

lessons.title: Deviations to the Main Line Part 2: White's Nf4 Ideas

r2qk1nr/pp1n1ppp/2pbp1b1/8/2BP1P2/6N1/PP.text:
9.f4 is White’s surprising idea, switching from Nf4 to f4 instead. 

If 9.Nf4, we can try our fancy 9...Qh4!? again or the simpler ...Ngf6.

r2qk2r/pp1n2pb/2pbBn1p/8/3P3P/6N1/PPP2PP.text: White places the rook on the open e-file, setting up potential discoveries.

r2qk2r/pp1nnppp/2pbp1b1/8/2BP1P2/6N1/PPP.text:
We continue with 9...Ne7! 

The whole point of delaying ...Ngf6 is revealed: we now control the light squares and completely prevent f4–f5.

r3k2r/ppqn2pb/2pbBn1p/8/3P3P/6N1/PPP2PP1.text:
We don’t fear any ghost checks and play 13...Qc7, leaving White without meaningful discovered attacks. 

Our plan is to castle long, forcing White to give a check with the bishop to stop it. 

With all our pieces developed, our extra piece comfortably outweighs White’s initiative. With solid defense, you will convert the win.

r3kb1r/pp1n1pp1/2p1pnp1/8/3P3q/2P2QN1/PP.text:
We recapture the piece, keeping our structure solid.

With our development secure, a key idea here is the e5 break to activate our pieces further.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnN1/8/3P3q/2P2QN1/PP.text: White eventually decides to take our bishop with 10.Nxg6.

r3kbnr/pp1n1ppp/2p1p1b1/8/3P1N1q/2P2QN1/.text:
White improves the queen to f3 to support the knight. 

We continue developing by bringing our king's knight out to f6.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppb/2pbBn1p/8/3P1N1P/6N1/PPP.text:
Our final move is simply to castle short. 

The e-file will now cost White a piece with no attacking chances.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppb/2pbpn1p/8/2BP1N1P/2P3N1/.text: The game may continue with White reinforcing the center.

rn1qk1nr/pp3pp1/2pbp1bp/8/2BP1N1P/6N1/PP.text:
White executes the knight jump to f4. 

We take on f4, expediting development at the cost of the bishops. 

However, White’s king lacks a safe home, with the kingside weakened by the h-pawn and the queenside facing a potential pawn storm and the bishop on g6.

rn1qk1nr/pp3ppp/2pbp1b1/8/2BP1N2/6N1/PPP.text: White continues with the main idea, 8.Nf4.

rn1qk1nr/pp3ppp/2pbp1b1/8/2BP3P/6N1/PPP1.text:
The aggressive 8.h4 has scored well for White. 

We respond by creating a retreat square with 8...h6.

rn1qk1nr/pp3ppp/2pbp1b1/8/2BP4/6N1/PPP1N.text:
White castles short, a flexible move that delays Nf4. 

We respond with 8...Nd7, once again keeping the kingside knight on g8 a bit longer.

rn1qk2r/pp3pp1/2p1pnbp/8/2BP1B1P/6N1/PPP.text:
We end the variation by completing our kingside development.

White’s king will be under pressure on either side of the board since we kept the g6-bishop alive.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppb/2pbBn1p/8/3P1N1P/6N1/PPP1.text:
Capturing on e6 is far too ambitious.

11.Ngh5 would have been the better try, after which we could trade and defend with ...Rg8, or even go 11...0-0 with a fighting middlegame ahead.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppb/2pbNn1p/8/2BP3P/6N1/PPP2P.text:
White goes for a famous Tal-style sacrifice, but it simply doesn’t work. 

We accept the free piece by capturing the knight.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppb/2pbpn1p/8/2BP1N1P/6N1/PPP.text:
11.Re1 is a calmer but stronger move, lining the rook up with our king. 

We are now just in time to castle short, despite all of White’s pressure on e6.

rn1qk2r/pp4pb/2pbBn1p/8/3P3P/6N1/PPP2PP1.text:
White takes on e6 with the bishop, gaining two pawns for the knight. 

Our king remains in the center, so White has some compensation, but we can defend. 

We continue with calm development, 12...Nbd7.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppb/2p1pn1p/8/2BP1N1P/6N1/PP.text:
White can also go full aggro with 10.Qe2, aiming to sacrifice on e6 at any cost. 

We answer with 10...Bd6, a very safe move, though 10...Qxd4 is also an option if you want to check.

White castles short, preparing Re1. 

We answer with 10...Bd6, adding pressure to the knight on f4.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p3bp/8/3P3P/6NN/PPP2PP.text:
In this study we examine 7.Nh3, a dangerous alternative to the main move 7.Nf3, aiming to attack the bishop via f4. 

We continue with the typical Caro push 7...e6, preparing development.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/8/2BP4/6N1/PPP2PP.text:
Bringing the bishop out to c4 is active and flexible. 

6.Bc4 is played only 3% of the time, yet it’s the third most popular move. 

We blunt the bishop with 6...e6, also preparing development.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/8/3P3P/6N1/PPP2PP.text:
Our main line in this study begins with 6.h4, pushing the h-pawn to trap our bishop. 

This move is played 32% of the time and is the second most popular. 

We respond with 6...h6, creating an escape square.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/8/3P4/6N1/PPP1NPP.text:
6.N1e2 will transpose into 6.Nh3 shortly after. 

This move is played only 3% of the time.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/8/3P4/6NN/PPP2PPP.text:
White plays 6.Nh3, aiming for Nf4 while keeping Bc4 ideas in reserve. 

This is an instructive plan but played only 2% of the time. 

We answer with 6...e6, always choosing ...e6 before ...Nf6 to keep our flexibility.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5b2/3P4/6N1/PPP2PPP.text:
The knight retreats to g3 with tempo on our bishop. 

We slide the bishop back to g6 for safety. From here, we focus on White’s aggressive Nf4 ideas, which can arise through Nh3, Ne2, h4, or even Bc4. 

Many of these move orders transpose, but you’ll be fully equipped to defend the Caro’s honor.

rn1qkbnr/pp3pp1/2p1p1bp/8/3P1N1P/6N1/PPP.text:
White completes the knight maneuver with 8.Nf4, attacking our bishop. 

We calmly retreat to h7, avoiding doubled pawns and preserving our good bishop.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppb/2p1p2p/8/2BP1N1P/6N1/PPP.text:
White develops the bishop to c4, the most aggressive approach, trying to make sacrifices on e6 work. 

As long as we develop accurately, we have nothing to fear. 

We meet the pressure with 9...Nf6, while White may aim at e6 with the queen or rook.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p1b1/8/2BP4/6N1/PPP1N.text:
White plays 7.N1e2, developing and hinting at Nf4. 

We answer with 7...Bd6, a flexible move that eyes the f4 square while delaying ...Nf6 for extra flexibility.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p1b1/8/3P1N2/6N1/PPP2.text:
White carries out the main idea with 7.Nf4; instead, 7.Bc4 Bd6 8.Nf4 Qh4!? is our quirky line to attack f4 and prevent h4. 

Here we immediately respond with 7...Qh4, disrupting White’s h4 plans and pressuring the fourth rank. 

Another idea was 7...Bd6 or ...Qc7 to target the Nf4.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p1b1/8/3P4/6N1/PPP1NP.text: We reply with 6...e6, and now White can go Nf4, fully transposing to the 6.Nh3 line.

rn1qr1k1/pp3ppb/2pbpn1p/8/2BP1N1P/2P3N1/.text:
We end the variation with 12...Re8, safeguarding e6.

...Nd7 and ...Qc7 are common follow-ups, and the e5 break is on the agenda.

rn2k1nr/pp3ppp/2pbp1b1/8/2BP1N1q/6N1/PPP.text:
Our solution is 8...Qh4!, an unusual but thematic move in this line. 

The queen not only targets the f4-knight but also prevents h4–h5 from chasing our bishop. 

We even encourage White to capture on g6 so that after hxg6 the h-file opens. ...Nf6, ...Nd7, and ...0-0-0 are natural follow-ups.

rn2kbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p1b1/8/3P1N1q/2P3N1/PP.text:
White protects the d4-pawn. 

We simply develop with 8...Nd7, as if nothing happened.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White grabs maximum central control with 2.d4. 

We contest the center with 2...d5, forming our typical light-square Caro structure.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
White chooses the Classical Caro with 3.Nc3, defending the center while developing. 

We take on e4, opening the position so our pieces can activate quickly.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
White recaptures with the knight. 

After 4...Bf5, we enter the Capablanca Caro, gaining a tempo on the knight with a developing bishop move.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Our previous study covered early sidelines and deviations from White. 

Now we go deeper into aggressive ideas that often involve Nf4, reached via h3 or e2. 

White begins by taking the center with 1.e4. 

As always, we reply 1...c6, entering the Caro-Kann.

1r5r/p2nkpp1/4pn1p/N1p4P/3q4/Q7/PPPN1PP1.text: White’s knight finally escapes the b7 square to a5, hoping for a royal fork on c6.

1r5r/pN1nkpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3q4/Q7/PPPN1PP1.text:
White unpins with tempo by checking our king. 

We choose the simple defense 19...c5, blocking the check with the pawn.

1rr5/p2nkpp1/4pn1p/N1p4P/3q4/Q7/PPPN1PP1.text:
We cover the Nc6 threat with 20...Rhc8. 

Our king is ready to step away without any trouble at all.

r2qkbnr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/7P/3P1B2/3Q1NN1/.text:
In this study we focus on 11.Bf4, the former main line and a very natural move. 

Our answer is 11...Qa5+, a slightly surprising check. 

The queen is excellently placed on a5, discouraging long castling due to pressure on a2 and also eyeing the advanced h5 pawn.

r2qkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p3bp/7P/3P4/5NN1/PPP2P.text:
White continues the plan by advancing the h-pawn. 

We fall back to the safe square we prepared.

r2qkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p4p/7P/3P4/3Q1NN1/PPP2.text:
White recaptures with the queen. 

We play 10...e6, building our sturdy light-square pawn formation that holds White’s pieces at bay. 

Now White must choose where to develop the dark-squared bishop: actively to f4 or more cautiously to d2.

r2qkbnr/pp1npppb/2p4p/7P/3P4/3B1NN1/PPP2.text:
White decides it’s time to trade our strong bishop and plays 9.Bd3. 

We accept the exchange.

r3k1nr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/q6P/1b1P1B2/2P2NN.text: White is forced to block the attack on the queen with 13.c3, hitting our bishop so as not to lose the queen.

r3k1nr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/q6P/1b1P4/2PQ1NN1.text:
White’s most common response is to kick our bishop with the c-pawn. 

We retreat to e7, a safe but influential square.

r3k1nr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/q6P/1b1P4/P2Q1NN1.text:
White can choose to force trades with 13.a3. 

We are forced to capture on d2.

r3k1nr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/q6P/1b1PN3/3Q1N2/.text:
White can try the tricky 13.Ne4, threatening Nd6+ thanks to the pin on our bishop. 

Our solution is simple: 13...Ngf6, a strong reply that calmly ignores the threat.

r3k1nr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/q6P/3P4/P2Q2N1/1P.text:
White recaptures with the knight, a more ambitious choice than 14.Qxd2, after which we could trade queens and develop calmly with ...Ngf6, ...Ke7, ...Rhd8, ...Rac8, and eventually ...c5. 

We continue developing with 14...Ngf6.

r3k1nr/pp1nbpp1/2p1p2p/q6P/2PP4/3Q1NN1/P.text:
White pushes the c-pawn again, trying to chase our Qa5. 

Other moves could be met by ...Ngf6 and ...0-0. 

We now retreat the queen to c7, having successfully encouraged White to play c4. 

Our whole idea is to strike with ...b5 and fight for the light squares.

r3k1nr/pp1nbpp1/2p1p2p/q6P/3P1B2/2P2NN1/.text:
We finish the line by retreating the bishop to e7. 

Now White can’t play c4 again because of ...Bb4, and we keep our strong queen on a5. 

White also can’t castle long, and if 14.0-0, then simply ...Ngf6 develops and eyes h5.

r3k1nr/ppqnbpp1/2p1p2p/7P/2PP4/3Q1NN1/PP.text:
White finally castles now that the queen has been pushed back. 

We complete development with 15...Ngf6. 

Having provoked c4, we’ll look to counter with ...b5, even at the cost of a pawn.

r3k2r/p1qnbpp1/2p1pn1p/1p5P/2PPN3/3Q1N2/.text:
And here comes 16...b5!, opening the queenside. 

If White pushes c5, we gain a beautiful d5 outpost. 

16...0-0 was also possible, keeping the b5/c5 strikes in hand after something like ...Rad8. 

This middlegame is rich, but our counterplay is fully adequate and our chances are no worse.

r3k2r/pp1n1pp1/2p1pn1p/q6P/3P4/P2Q2N1/1P.text: The a2 pawn is not hanging, so White can safely castle long.

r3k2r/pp1n1pp1/2pNpn1p/q6P/1b1P4/3Q1N2/P.text:
White goes for the check. 

After 14... Ke7, our king may look adventurous, but White has no attacking resources to punish it.

r3k2r/ppqnbpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/2PPN3/3Q1N2/PP.text:
A possible continuation is this knight jump to e4, centralizing while hinting at g4–g5 ideas. 

Instead, 16.Kb1 can be met with 16...0-0, keeping ...Rd8 and the ...b5/...c5 breaks in reserve.

r3kb1r/pp1n1pp1/2p1pn1p/1Q5P/1P1P1B2/2P2.text: White accepts the queen trade and uses the chance to double our pawns.

r3kb1r/pp1n1pp1/2p1pn1p/q6P/1P1P1B2/2PQ1.text:
White might get frustrated and try to chase the queen with 13.b4. 

We answer with 13...Qb5, an interesting idea; other queen moves were also perfectly fine.

r3kb1r/pp1n1pp1/4pn1p/1p5P/1P1P1B2/2P2NN.text:
We recapture with the c-pawn. 

This exchange gives us excellent light-square outposts and the open c-file to pressure c3.

r3kbnr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/q6P/3P1B2/2PQ1NN1.text:
White can choose the simple way to block the check with 12.c3, but our queen remains perfectly placed. 

We keep things calm with 12...Ngf6, just developing, and White still can’t castle on either side because of the a2 and h5 pawns.

r3kbnr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/q6P/3P1B2/5NN1/PP.text:
White gets scared and offers a queen trade by blocking the check with the queen. 

We decline the exchange and develop our bishop to b4, keeping our queen active.

r3kbnr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/q6P/3P4/3Q1NN1/PP.text:
White blocks the check and attacks the queen with 12.Bd2. 

In earlier days Black would retreat with ...Qc7, but not anymore. 12...Bb4 keeps the queen active a bit longer.

r4rk1/pp1n1pp1/2p1pn1p/q6P/3P4/P2Q2N1/1P.text:
We also castle, but short. 

We reach a balanced position where we may look for chances to attack White’s king.

r6r/pN1nkpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/1q1P4/1Q6/PPPN1P.text:
White plays 17.Qb3, saving the knight but allowing us to win the d4 pawn. 

If 17.Qa3, queens come off and we simply place rooks on b8 and c8 before pushing ...c5; the extra pawn is irrelevant. 

We capture on d4, recovering our pawn.

r6r/pN1nkpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3q4/1Q6/PPPN1PP1.text:
White castles long, setting up a few discovered knight tricks, but none are dangerous. 

We respond by pinning the knight to the queen with our a-rook and preparing to walk the king to safety.

r6r/pN1nkpp1/2p1pn1p/q6P/1b1P4/3Q1N2/PPP.text:
White grabs the b7 pawn, abandoning the knight. 

Instead, after 15.Nc4 Bxd2+ 16.Nfxd2 Qc7, we would be perfectly safe with ...Rhd8 and ...c5, followed by ...Kf8–Kg8 if needed. 

Here we start by trading off the pinned bishop.

r6r/pN1nkpp1/2p1pn1p/q6P/3P4/3Q4/PPPN1PP.text:
White recaptures with the knight. 

If 16.Qxd2, then 16...Qb5 traps the knight on b7 (17.Na5 Ne4!). 

Now we play 16...Qb4, a key move that attacks the Nb7 and also stops Qa3+.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p3bp/8/3P3P/5NN1/PPP2P.text:
White develops with 7.Nf3, which also threatens Ne5. 

We acknowledge the threat and play 7...Nd7, a solid move that prevents Ne5; the more provocative 7...e6 is playable, but the old main line has proven reliable.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/8/3P3P/6N1/PPP2PP.text:
White plays 6.h4, trying to gain time and space against our well-placed bishop. 

We reply 6...h6, guaranteeing an escape square in case of h5.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5b2/3P4/6N1/PPP2PPP.text:
The knight retreats to g3, attacking our bishop. 

We retreat to g6, keeping the bishop on a strong diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White builds a broad center with 2.d4.

We immediately fight back with 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
White enters the Classical Variation with 3.Nc3. 

As always, we take in the center, luring the knight to e4 so we can gain time attacking it.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
White recaptures with the knight. 

We enter the Capablanca Variation with 4...Bf5, developing the bishop with tempo.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In this study we dive into the heart of the topical Classical Capablanca variations. 

If you check databases for White’s 11.Bf4, you’ll see it was once a major option with tens of thousands of games, though in the past decade players have mostly switched to 11.Bd2 (next study). 

Still, 11.Bf4 is a good move, and we must know the key ideas to reach a strong middlegame. 

White begins by taking the center with 1.e4. 

We reply 1...c6, preparing the Caro light-square pawn chain.

r2q1rk1/pp1nbpp1/2p1p2p/7P/3PQ3/5N2/PPPB.text:
White recaptures with the queen. 

We improve our other knight to f6, gaining a tempo on the queen.

r2q1rk1/pp1nbpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3PN3/3Q1N2/P.text:
White continues with 14.Ne4, a common plan since the knight on g3 is misplaced and the g-pawn needs room to advance. 

We trade on e4 to gain tempi.

r2q1rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3P4/5N2/PPPBQ.text:
White’s queen slips back to e2, preparing an attack. 

It’s our moment to centralize: 16...Qd5, a key idea in this variation. 

From d5 the queen is perfectly placed for both attack and defense.

r2qk2r/pp1nbpp1/2p1p2p/7P/3PQ3/5N2/PPPB1.text:
White recaptures with the queen. 

As in the main line, we use our other knight to gain a tempo on the queen with 14...Nf6.

r2qk2r/pp1nbpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3P4/3Q1NN1/PP.text:
White has many options, but the most popular and flexible is 13.Kb1, stepping out of danger and covering a2. 

We castle short, and the opposite-side castling battle begins.

r2qk2r/pp1nbpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3P4/5NN1/PPPB.text:
13.Qe2 is an interesting retreat. White makes room for the d1-rook to gain influence.

We respond immediately with 13...c5!, striking the center and, more importantly, opening the c-file for future counterplay.

r2qk2r/pp1nbpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3PN3/3Q1N2/PP.text:
Putting the knight on e4 is a typical maneuver for White, bringing the passive Ng3 back to the center while opening the door for g4–g5 ideas. 

We meet it by trading on e4.

r2qk2r/pp1nbpp1/4pn1p/2P4P/8/5NN1/PPPBQP.text: White captures on c5, exchanging in the center.

r2qk2r/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3P4/5N2/PPPBQP.text:
The queen retreats to e2, a safe square. 

If 15.Qd3, then c5!? is an interesting way to break open the center and the c-file. 

As in the main sequence, we improve our queen to d5 once White’s queen returns to e2, a typical motif in this variation and the reason White often plays Kb1 early to protect a2. 

If you prefer avoiding queen trades, 15...a5!? is a fun alternative, aiming to provoke weaknesses with a4–a3.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1pp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3P4/3Q1NN1/P.text:
White proceeds with long castling. 

Compared to the 11.Bf4 lines, you’ll notice how much easier it is for White to castle quickly here, which is why 11.Bd2 has grown in popularity. 

We answer with 12...Be7, a revolutionary idea in the Caro: Black is going to play actively and castle short. 

The older approach with 12...Qc7 followed by 0-0-0 gave the Caro a solid but dull reputation. 

The discovery that castling short is sound sparked huge interest, attracting even attacking players to this variation.

r2qkbnr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/7P/3P4/3Q1NN1/PP.text:
The more modest development 11.Bd2 has become the modern main line. 

Its purpose is simple: stop ...Qa5+ and clear the way for long castling. 

Our reply is nothing fancy, 11...Ngf6, the knight’s best square by far.

r2qkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p3bp/7P/3P4/5NN1/PPP2P.text:
White pushes the h-pawn again. 

We drop the bishop back to the square we prepared in advance.

r2qkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p4p/7P/3P4/3Q1NN1/PPP2.text:
White recaptures with the queen. 

We reinforce our center with 10...e6, building the trademark Caro light-square structure that restricts White’s activity.

r2qkbnr/pp1npppb/2p4p/7P/3P4/3B1NN1/PPP2.text:
White decides to trade our active bishop with 9.Bd3. 

We accept the trade.

r2r2k1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/5q1P/2PP4/5N2/PP1.text: Our final move is 18...Rfd8, preparing strong counterplay with the upcoming ...c5.

r3k2r/pp2b1p1/2p1p2p/5p1P/2PPn3/4BN2/PP3.text:
We choose the most aggressive option in this position: 18...f5!, aiming to push ...f4 and target f2. 

If 19.g3, then ...Bg5! followed by hxg5 is excellent for us. 

Instead, 18...b5!? was another counterplay option, and the solid 18...0-0 with ...Rd8, ...Rc8, and ...c5 at the right moment was also perfectly playable.

r3k2r/pp2bpp1/2p1p2p/7P/2PPn3/4BN2/PP3PP.text: White defends the f2 pawn, stopping any trades or forks.

r3k2r/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/3q3P/2PP4/5N2/PP1B.text:
White covers a2 with tempo using 16.c4, attacking our queen. 

We step forward to e4, offering a queen trade. 

If White declines with 17.Be3, our queen stays very active; a strong reply is 17...b5!, immediately launching an attack on the king. 

A funny detail is that after 18.Rh4!? Qh7! the queen becomes extremely annoying for White.

r3k2r/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/2PPQ3/5N2/PP1B1.text:
White accepts and trades queens. 

We recapture with the knight.

r3k2r/ppqnbpp1/4pn1p/2P4P/8/5NN1/PPPBQPP.text:
We don’t recapture on c5 right away and instead play 14...Qc7, a clean sidestep out of the Rd1 line. 

Now we’ll be ready to castle and recapture on c5 with strong counterplay.

r4rk1/pp2b1p1/2p1p2p/5p1P/3Pq1n1/4BN2/PP.text: We answer with 19...f5, and everything is protected, we’re simply a pawn up!

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1p2p/3nN2P/3Pq1P1/4B3/PP.text:
White pushes ahead with 19.g4, insisting on the attack. 

But we have counterplay ready with ...c5!

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1p2p/7P/3Pq1n1/4BN2/PPP1.text: White brings the d-rook to the semi-open file, attacking our knight and lining it up with our king.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/1q5P/2PP4/4BN2/PP2.text:
White again declines the queen trade and hits our queen with the c-pawn. 

If we had traded on b5, we would gain excellent light-square control and strong queenside play with …Rc8 and …Nd5. 

Now we give the queen check on f5, the very reason we wanted to provoke c4.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/3q3P/2PP4/5N2/PP1B.text:
17.c4 looks tempting to attack our queen, but it actually weakens White’s king. 

This lets us slide to f5 with check, placing the queen on a very active square.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/3q3P/3P2P1/5N2/PPP.text:
White begins pushing the kingside pawns with 17.g4, a dangerous move signaling an attack. 

We immediately react by offering a queen trade for safety with 17...Qe4.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/3q3P/3P4/4BN2/PPP1.text:
White’s idea behind 17.Be3 is to anticipate …Qe4 and, to a lesser extent, bring the Rd1 into play. 

If given time, White will push g4, possibly combined with Ne5. 

We still ask for a queen trade with 17...Qb5, trying to provoke a weakness.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/3qN2P/3P4/8/PPPBQP.text:
White plays 17.Ne5, a strong centralizing move that supports the plan f4–g4–g5. 

We offer a queen trade with 17...Qe4 to blunt White’s attacking chances.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/4N2P/3Pq3/4B3/PPP1.text:
White declines the trade with 18.Be3!, keeping queens on and playing for the attack.

If 18.Qxe4 Nxe4 19.Be3 Rfd8, we continue with ...Rac8 and time ...c5 correctly; White’s extra space is balanced by our solid structure and good piece activity.

Here we use the pin on the bishop to play 18...Nd5, preventing f3 from kicking us away.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/5q1P/2PP4/4BN2/PP2.text: The king slides to a1, stepping into safety.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/5q1P/2PP4/5N2/PP1B.text: The king slides to b1, retreating to safety.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/7P/3Pq1P1/4BN2/PPP.text:
White declines the trade and blocks with the bishop, sacrificing the g4 pawn. 

If 18.Qxe4? Nxe4 19.Be3 f5! White would already be in serious trouble due to the ...f4 threat (and if 20.gxf5, then ...Rxf5 wins a pawn). 

We calmly take the free pawn with the knight.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/4p2p/2pnN2P/3Pq1P1/4B3/PPP.text:
As planned, 19...c5 hits the board. 

White’s center comes under heavy pressure, making any g5 attack unsound. 

We can increase the pressure with ...Rc8 or ...Rd8, reaching a comfortable and dynamic position.

r4rk1/pp2bpp1/4pn1p/2p2q1P/2PP4/4BN2/PP2.text:
And here comes our central counterplay with 19...c5! 

The queen’s pendulum maneuver has successfully provoked weaknesses around White’s king, and we strike at the perfect moment.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p3bp/8/3P3P/5NN1/PPP2P.text:
White continues developing with 7.Nf3, which also hints at Ne5. 

We meet this with 7...Nd7, a solid developing move that covers e5; the sharper 7...e6 is playable but less solid.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/8/3P3P/6N1/PPP2PP.text:
White plays 6.h4, hoping to seize space and harass our bishop. 

We calmly reply with 6...h6, securing a safe square in case of h5.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5b2/3P4/6N1/PPP2PPP.text:
The knight drops back to g3, eyeing our bishop. 

We respond by retreating to g6, keeping the bishop on a powerful diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White expands in the center with 2.d4. 

We immediately challenge this with 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
With 3.Nc3, White enters the Classical Variation. 

As usual, we capture on e4, tempting the knight forward so we can gain time by targeting it.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
White recaptures with the knight. 

We choose the Capablanca Variation with 4...Bf5, developing our bishop while hitting the knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
The final study of our chapter dives into a long main line that became a hallmark of the modern Classical Caro - one that often leads to opposite-side castling and sharp play.

White begins by staking out the center with 1.e4. 

We answer with 1...c6, setting up the Caro’s solid light-square structure.

r1bq1bkr/pp4p1/2n1pnNp/2p5/2BP4/2P5/PP3P.text: White avoids the trade and attacks our rook with 11.Ng6.

r1bq1bkr/pp4p1/2n1pnNp/8/2Bp4/2P5/PP3PPP.text:
We can simply give up the rook for the knight - we’re up so much material that it doesn’t matter.

We take in the center with 11...cxd4.

r1bq1rk1/p3bppp/1pn1pn2/2p5/2B2B2/3P1NN1.text: Since we played 7...e6 with our light-squared bishop still inside the pawn chain, we look to fianchetto it with 10...b6.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2p5/2B2B2/3P1NN1.text: White develops the last minor piece, bringing the bishop out to f4.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2p5/2B5/3P1NN1/PP.text:
White plays 9.d3, both sides are simply completing development at this point. 

Note that White could have played d3 earlier, since the idea is purely developmental. 

We now castle.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2p5/2B5/5NN1/PPPP.text:
White castles. 

We consolidate our structure with 7...e6, keeping the light-squared bishop inside the pawn chain for now.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2p5/2B5/5NN1/PPPP.text:
White places the rook on the semi-open e-file. 

We continue developing with 8...Be7, preparing to castle.

r3k2r/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/q4b2/2BP4/2P2N2/PP2.text:
White builds a sturdy pawn chain with 11.c3. 

Both sides are solid and developing naturally, so the position is roughly equal.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/q4b2/2BP4/5N2/PPP1.text:
White takes the center with 10.d4. 

We calmly continue developing with 10...Be7, reaching a very solid position.

r3kb1r/pp1npppp/2p5/q4b2/2B5/5N2/PPPPQPP.text:
White castles short. 

We respond with a typical Caro move, 9...e6, preparing to finish our kingside development.

r4rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/q4b2/2BP1Q2/2P2N2/P.text: We complete development with 11...Nd7, reaching a very comfortable position to end the variation.

r4rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/q4b2/2BP4/2P2N2/PP2.text:
We finish by castling, completing development. 

From here, we can consider queenside play with ...b5 or ...a5, and we’ll also place our rooks on the e- and d-files.

rn1qr1k1/p3bppp/2p1bp2/1p6/3P4/4BN2/PPP1.text: With opposite-side castling on the board, we go for 10...b5, not only preparing a pawn storm but also opening the door for ...Qd5, which directly threatens the king.

rn1qr1k1/pp2bppp/2p1bp2/8/3P4/4BN2/PPP1Q.text: White defends the a2 pawn by sliding the king to b1.

rn2k2r/pp2bppp/2p1p3/q4b2/2B2Q2/2P2N2/PP.text:
A typical continuation for White is 10.c3, preparing d4. 

We simply get to safety and prepare to bring our knight out next.

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/q4b2/2B2Q2/5N2/PPPP1.text:
White’s most common option is to keep the queen active by sliding it to f4. 

We continue with 8...e6, preparing further development and keeping a very solid position.

We’re completely comfortable after our pieces come out via e7 and d7, followed by castling. 

Be cautious about grabbing the c2 pawn if White offers it, d3! can strand our bishop.

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/q4b2/2B5/5N2/PPPPQPP.text:
White can also opt for a safe and solid retreat with 8.Qe2. 

We continue with normal development by playing 8...Nd7.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/q4b2/2B2Q2/5N2/PPPP.text:
White castles. 

We prepare to castle as well by developing our kingside with 9...Be7.

rn3rk1/pp2bppp/2p1p3/q4b2/2BP1Q2/2P2N2/P.text: White establishes a central pawn with 11.d4.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3q4/1P2Q3/5N2/P1PP1.text: We escape the danger by sliding to d5, offering a queen trade while still keeping ...Bf5 in reserve if the queen moves away from e4.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/q7/1P2Q3/5N2/P1PP1P.text: An interesting and active solution for White is 7.b4, aiming to chase our queen.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/q7/2B1Q3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
White often continues with the logical developing move 7.Bc4. 

As planned, we play 7...Bf5, developing with tempo on the queen.

rnbq1b1r/pp2pkp1/2p2n1p/8/2B5/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
White continues with the ambitious 7.Bc4+, developing with check. 

We calmly block with 7...e6.

rnbq1b1r/pp3kp1/2p1pn1p/4N3/2B5/8/PPPP1P.text:
White keeps up the aggressive style with 8.Ne5+, checking our king again. 

We retreat to g8, where the king is perfectly safe.

rnbq1bkr/pp4p1/2p1pn1p/4N3/2BP4/8/PPP2PP.text:
With no immediate threats left, White prepares to bring more pieces into the game by occupying the center with 9.d4. 

We counter the center and prepare development with 9...c5.

rnbq1bkr/pp4p1/4pn1p/2p1N3/2BP4/2P5/PP3P.text:
White reinforces the center with 10.c3. 

We strike back with 10...Nc6, targeting the center and offering trades.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p2p2/8/3P4/4BN2/PPP1QP.text:
With 8.Be3, White prepares to castle long. 

We answer by sliding the rook to the open e-file, lining it up against the enemy queen and king.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/2p2p2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1QPPP.text:
White now decides to seize the center with 7.d4. 

It’s time for us to get our king to safety.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pNp1/2p2n1p/8/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White’s whole idea is to sacrifice on f7, but there’s nowhere near enough support for the attack. 

We take the knight for free.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2N2/8/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
White also has the option to capture on f6, but this is exactly what we want! 

It’s the most common move, played in about 46% of games. 

We recapture with the e-pawn, and now the position strongly resembles a Tartakower. 

In fact, after White’s natural 6.d4, the game transposes.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/6N1/8/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Declining the trade with 5.Neg5 is not a good move, but some tricky players may go for a quick attack, which simply doesn’t work. 

Still, about 4% of players will try it.

We immediately respond with 5...h6, kicking the knight away.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/4N3/5N2/PPPPQPP.text:
White’s main line is the tricky 5.Qe2, which keeps the game in true Two Knights spirit. 

This move is fairly common, played in about 19% of games, and we need to know how to counter it.

Our solution is to take on e4, removing the central tension; just don’t blunder with something like 5...Nbd7?? allowing 6.Nd6 mate.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/8/5NN1/PPPP1PPP.text:
Declining the knight trade and retreating to g3 is a passive but solid option, White chooses it about 20% of the time. 

We reply with the interesting idea 5...c5, preventing White from playing d4.

Next we’ll develop with ...e6, ...Nc6, ...Be7, ...0-0, and even ...b6–Bb7.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/8/4Q3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
White is forced to recapture with the queen. 

Here we have an interesting idea: 6...Qa5, preparing ...Bf5 while also preventing d4 by pinning the pawn to the king.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p5/2B5/5NN1/PPPP1P.text:
White may continue with normal development via 6.Bc4, aiming at f7 and making it harder for us to develop the light-squared bishop to g4. 

We simply keep developing with 6...Nc6, controlling the d4 square.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2p2/8/8/5N2/PPPPQPPP/R.text:
White tries to take control of the open e-file early with 6.Qe2+, but this check doesn’t bother us at all.

We simply develop our dark-squared bishop to e7, blocking the check.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
White develops the knight with 2.Nc3, controlling the center. 

For the purposes of the Two Knights, 2.Nf3 and 2.Nc3 are interchangeable, as both moves transpose.

We continue by building the solid Caro pawn chain with 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
White plays 3.Nf3, officially entering the Two Knights Caro, using both knights to control the center. 

As noted in the introduction, we capture on e4 with 3...dxe4, aiming to steer the game into Tartakower territory.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/4N3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
White recaptures on e4 with the knight. 

We continue with another typical Tartakower move, 4...Nf6, offering the knight trade and not worrying about doubled f-pawns.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the Two Knights Caro chapter. 

The Two Knights is a very sound and solid system for White, quickly bringing out two knights as the name suggests. 

In this study we’ll examine a possible transposition into the Tartakower (if that’s your weapon against the Classical). 

The game begins with 1.e4, placing a pawn in the center.

As always we reply with 1...c6, preparing the Caro counter.

rnbqr1k1/pp2bppp/2p2p2/8/3P4/4BN2/PPP1QP.text:
White castles long. 

We continue developing with 9...Be6, angling our bishops toward the queenside.

r1b1k1nr/pp1n1ppp/1qp5/2b1P3/4BP2/8/PPP1.text:
White recaptures the pawn. 

We undermine e5 with 8...f6.

If White captures on f6, then after ...Nfxf6, our pieces flood the board.

r1b1k1nr/pp1n1ppp/1qp5/2bpP3/4PB2/5P2/PP.text: We end the variation with 6...Qb6, with a strong double attack.

r1b1k1nr/pp1n1ppp/1qp5/2bpP3/4PP2/3B4/PP.text:
White defends e5 with their f-pawn.

Our response is to open the center with 7...dxe4.

r1b1k1nr/pp1n2pp/1qp1Pp2/2b5/4BP2/8/PPP1.text:
Pushing the e-pawn to attack the knight looks tempting but loses. 

It's time for us to check the king with our bishop, 9...Bf2+, clearing the c5 square for our knight.

r1b1k1nr/pp1n2pp/1qp1Pp2/8/4BP2/8/PPP1Nb.text: White's king is forced to f1 since 10. Kd2 Qe3 is mate!

r1b1k1nr/pp4pp/1qp1Pp2/2n5/4BP2/8/PPP1Nb.text:
We escape danger by playing 10...Nc5. 

We will get our pawn back with massive development and a winning position.

r1b1k2r/pp1n2pp/2p2n2/2b5/4pP2/2N5/PPP3P.text: After 9...Bc5 we already have a better position because of the edge in development.

r1b1kb1r/pp1n2pp/2p2n2/8/4pP2/2N5/PPP3PP.text: White can continue developing, trying to come back into the game.

r1b1kbnr/pp1n1ppp/2p5/4P3/4pP2/8/PPP3PP/.text:
White supports e5 with their f-pawn.

We immediately undermine the structure by playing 7...f6.

White’s position is under fire; if Nf2, we play ...fxe5 and enjoy superior development.

r1b1kbnr/pp1n2pp/2p2P2/8/4pP2/8/PPP3PP/R.text:
Most players decide to capture, which only speeds up our development.

We bring out the knight, developing and recapturing.

r1bq1rk1/1p2nppp/2p5/p1bpP3/1n2PP2/2NB1N.text:
We’re in no rush to take the bishop, so 9...a5 is our move. 

If a3, we take on d3; if exd5, we recapture with ...Nexd5.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n2n2/1B1p2B1/3Q4/2N2P2.text:
And we castle kingside.

Next, we'll activate our bishop to e6 to strengthen the center. The rook can occupy the semi-open c-file and the queen can activate to the queenside.

r1bq1rk1/pp2n1pp/2n2p2/1BbpP3/5P2/2N5/PP.text:
We undermine e5 with 9...f6, activating the rook and opening lines toward White’s king. 

Our bishop dominates from c5, and soon the queen and light-squared bishop will join the attack from b6 and g4.

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n5/1BbpP3/5P2/2N5/PPP1.text: White focuses on saving the pawn instead of developing.

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2p5/2bpP3/1n2PP2/2NB1N2.text: White develops the queen to e2, continuing to defend the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/n1p5/2bpP3/4PP2/2NB1N2/.text:
If White plays naturally with 8.Nf3 for example...

We can attack the bishop on d3 by playing 8...Nb4.

r1bqk1nr/pp1n1ppp/2p5/2bpP3/4PB2/5P2/PPP.text: White plays 6.Bf4 defending e5 but leaving b2 loose.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n5/1BbpP3/8/2N2P2/PPP1N.text:
White develops the last kingside minor piece but still can’t castle because of our dark-squared bishop. 

We castle ourselves, bringing the king to safety while also threatening ...Nxe5.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/1B1p2B1/3Q4/2N2P2/.text:
White develops their dark-squared bishop and pins our newly developed knight, removing the defender of the d5 pawn. 

But we easily unpin, 8...Be7 is next.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/1B1p4/3Q4/2N2P2/PPP3.text:
White continues developing and plays 7.Nc3, attacking d5. 

We defend calmly with 7...Nf6.

r3k1nr/pp3ppp/1qn5/3QP3/8/2N2P1P/PPP1K2P.text:
It's time for a sneaky intrusion! 

After 10...Bg1 we now we have serious threats of Qf2/Rd8.

rn2k1nr/pp3ppp/1q6/2bQP3/8/5P1P/PPP4P/RN.text:
White greedily grabs a pawn with the queen.

We can now take the chance to displace White's king. 8...Bf2+ is next.

rn2k1nr/pp3ppp/1q6/3QP3/8/5P1P/PPP1Kb1P/.text:
White moves their king up since the d-file is too dangerous with a future ...Rd8.

We continue with development, 9...Nc6, also setting up Rd8 ideas.

rn2k1nr/pp3ppp/1qp5/2bPP3/8/5P1P/PPP4P/R.text:
White recaptures the piece.

We continue by taking on d5, with obvious compensation as we complete development and White's king stays stranded in the center.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/1qp5/2bPP3/8/5P1N/PPP3PP.text:
White stops ...Bxg1 and ...Bf2+ simultaneously by playing 6.Nh3.

But we can now take on h3, not only eliminating the defender of f2 but also ruining White's pawn structure.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/1qp5/2bpP3/4P3/3B1P2/PPP.text:
White sidesteps our ...Bxg1 idea and develops the attacked knight to e2.

We also bring our knight out, 6...Nd7, developing with tempo.

rnb1k2r/1p2nppp/1qp5/p2pP3/4PP2/2N2N2/PP.text: We end the variation with 8...a5, a clever idea, opening the a7 square for the queen in case of Na4.

rnb1k2r/pp2nppp/1qp5/2bpP3/4PP2/2N2N2/PP.text:
White sidesteps the attack.

This only forces their king into the open after 7...Bf2+.

rnb1k2r/pp2nppp/1qp5/3pP3/4PP2/2N2N2/PPP.text: White plays the only move that works.

rnb1kbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/4P3/4p3/5P2/PPP3PP/R.text:
White recaptures with the knight to keep the option of castling.

We develop with 6...Nd7, attacking e5.

There’s no need to play ...exf3 and help White develop.

rnb1kbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/8/3PP2q/8/PP4PP/RNBQ.text: After we check the king with the queen, White loses the e-pawn!

rnbq1rk1/pp2nppp/2p5/2bpP3/4P3/2NB1P2/PP.text:
Developing with 7.Nge2 has been the most common continuation.

We continue developing while attacking e5. 7...Ng6 is next.

rnbq1rk1/pp2nppp/2p5/2bpP3/4PP2/2NB4/PPP.text:
White plays 7.f4, preparing Nf3, a computer-approved response. 

Even if White manages to stabilize, the exposed king on e1 gives us long-term compensation. 

We develop creatively, bringing our knight out to a6.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2p3n1/2bpP3/4PP2/2NB4/PP.text:
White defends e5 with their f-pawn.

Our next move is to jump forward with our g-knight, 8...Nh4, a nice idea to attack White's king.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2p5/2bpP3/4PP1n/2NB4/PPP.text: 9.Kf1 is forced since 9. g3?? Nf3+ 10. Kf1 Bh3 is mate!

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2p2p2/2bpP3/4PP1n/2NB4/PP.text:
Our final move in the variation is 9...f6, blowing up more files to attack White.

I like Black's attack more than White's pawn.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p5/2bPP3/8/5P2/PPP3PP/R.text:
Capturing on d5 is too greedy, although played 34% of the time.

Our response is to strike on the weak diagonal with 5...Qb6, the whole point of our gambit!

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p5/2bpP3/4P3/2N2P2/PPP3.text:
White’s best response is to keep developing with 5.Nc3, often followed by Na4 ideas. 

You’ll see this in about 38% of games. 

We continue developing normally with 5...Ne7.
